title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 53)
hookLine: Jewish tradition reads the servant as the people Israel in exile

lines: WHO IS HE? WHO ARE WE?
cards: Somebody in this chapter is speaking, and they sound stunned. Kings shut their mouths. A voice asks, Who hath believed our report?
And then a group starts to confess. We looked at him and saw nothing worth seeing. We turned our faces away.

We thought he was struck down by God. But he was wounded for what we had done. Isaiah fifty-three is written mostly in the voice of onlookers, realizing too late what they did to someone they despised.
The question it leaves: who is the someone? And who are we?

teach.h: A MAN OF PAINS, ACQUAINTED WITH DISEASE.
teach.b: The onlookers describe him: "He was despised, and forsaken of men, A man of pains, and acquainted with disease."

Wounded, bruised, led like a lamb, cut off, and yet in the end, the chapter says, he shall see his seed and prolong his days. So who is this servant? Jewish tradition answers from inside the book of Isaiah itself.
A few chapters earlier, the prophet names the servant outright: "Thou art My servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified." And again: But thou, Israel, art my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen.
Read that way, the servant in chapter fifty-three is the people Israel in exile: scattered, mocked, treated as if their suffering proved God had abandoned them.
And the we who speak are the nations, the kings who shut their mouths, finally seeing that the people they scorned carried more than their own share.
Some Jewish readers hear the righteous within Israel, or the prophet himself, and the ancient Aramaic translation, the Targum, reads the passage's opening verse as speaking of the Messiah.
Christians read this chapter as speaking of Jesus. The same words, read in different ways by two traditions, each with its own teachers and commentaries.
This path follows the Jewish reading, and notice what that reading does. It refuses the onlookers' first conclusion: he must have deserved it.

teach.h: SUFFERING IS NOT PROOF OF GUILT.
teach.b: Suffering is not proof of guilt.
A people can be despised and still be God's servant. Still be held. Still have a future.

how: Jews read Isaiah 52 and 53 as part of the book of Isaiah; Jewish commentators read the servant as the people Israel, and the passage is part of the conversation between Jews and Christians, who read it differently.

games.q: you're one of the onlookers. you watched a despised people suffer and assumed God had struck them. what does the chapter have you say?
o: we were wrong; we turned our faces away.
it had nothing to do with us.
games.why: the onlookers confess: they turned away and thought him stricken by God. the chapter turns their first conclusion around.

practice: Let one person or one people come to mind who are suffering and are blamed for it, the ones people say must have brought it on themselves.

If any part of you has quietly agreed, don't argue with it; just set it down, and stay with them a while, looking instead of turning away, the way the onlookers finally did. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
